opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this came out of the work we did at Uber AI on deconstructing lottery tickets. The original lottery ticket procedure is: you train a network, prune the weights with the smallest final magnitudes, then rewind the surviving weights to their initial values and retrain. The story people told was that you'd found a lucky subnetwork that was well suited to training from the start.

When we started pulling apart which ingredients actually mattered, we found something surprising. If you take that mask and apply it to the original random initialization, with no retraining, the network already performs far above chance. On MNIST you could get something like eighty or ninety percent accuracy just from the masked untrained network. That's what we called a supermask.

So the question became: why would zeroing out weights produce a working network? The way I came to think about it is that masking is itself an optimization operation. Setting a weight to zero is a choice about its value. If the mask criterion is correlated with where the weights would have gone in training, then you're pushing the network in a useful direction. The "large final" criterion keeps weights that grew in magnitude, and those tend to be the ones whose sign was already right. Weights that trained toward zero, or would have flipped sign, get set to zero. That's roughly the same move a gradient step makes. You're moving each weight closer to its trained value, just in a very coarse, binary way.

We tested that directly. We tried a version where we froze the pruned weights at their initial values instead of zeroing them. That hurt performance noticeably. But if you only froze them at zero when they'd moved toward zero during training, and kept the initial value otherwise, you recovered most of it. The zero itself carried information.

The signs also turned out to matter a lot. If you keep the mask and the signs of the initial weights but reinitialize the magnitudes, lottery tickets still work. If you randomize the signs, they break.

So that's why I'd say masking is a training step. Choosing which weights to keep based on information from a trained network leaks some of that training into the "untrained" subnetwork. We took it a step further and learned the masks directly with gradient descent, keeping the weights at random initialization. You can get surprisingly strong performance that way, which reinforces that selecting a subnetwork is a real form of learning. It's just learning in a different parameterization than the one we usually think about.

r001.rationale: It says applying the pruned mask to the original random initialization, with no retraining, performs far above chance (about 80–90% on MNIST).

r002.rationale: It explains that zeroing weights selected using training information moves them toward zero when training had moved them that way, approximating a useful training update.

r003.rationale: It says masks can be learned directly at random initialization and achieve strong performance, but does not suggest that finding lottery tickets without prior dense-model training is harder than expected.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the lottery ticket hypothesis, as Frankle and Carbin framed it, says that inside a large randomly initialized network there's a sparse subnetwork that, if you train it in isolation from the original initialization, reaches comparable accuracy to the full network. The way you find it is you train the dense network, prune the smallest-magnitude weights, reset the surviving weights to their initial values, and repeat.

The intuition people had was that the magic lived in the initialization: you'd found some lucky set of initial weights that happened to be trainable. What we did in the Deconstructing Lottery Tickets paper was pull apart which pieces actually mattered, and one of the things that popped out was that the mask on its own does a lot of work. If you take the winning ticket mask, apply it to the original random init, and don't train at all, the resulting network often performs far above chance. In some of our MNIST and CIFAR experiments you'd see these untrained "supermasks" hitting, you know, well above random, sometimes dramatically so.

So why do I call masking a training step? Think about what the pruning criterion is actually doing. The criterion that works best isn't just "keep the largest final magnitude," it's closely related to "keep the weights that moved away from zero," meaning the weights whose sign and direction after training agree with where they started. When you zero out a weight, you're not making a neutral choice; you're moving that parameter to the value zero. And for the weights you're pruning, zero is typically closer to where training wanted them to go than their random initial value was. In that sense, applying the mask is a very coarse, one-bit-per-weight version of a gradient step: for each weight you either leave it alone or you push it toward zero, and you choose based on information gathered from the training trajectory.

Once you frame it that way, the surprising supermask results stop looking mysterious. You've effectively done one extremely quantized optimization step over the whole network using information from a full training run. Of course that produces something better than random. And it also tells you the lottery ticket story isn't really about finding a special initialization; it's that the mask encodes training signal, and the init only matters insofar as the signs are preserved. We showed you could reinitialize the surviving weights to random values as long as you kept the original sign, and the ticket still worked. Change the signs and it falls apart.

So the short version is: a mask is a learned object. Treating it as "just" an architectural choice hides the fact that producing it required optimization, and applying it changes the function in a direction that optimization pointed to.

r001.rationale: It says applying the winning-ticket mask to the original random initialization, with no further training, can perform well above chance.

r002.rationale: It explains that for pruned weights, zero is typically closer to the value training wanted than the initial weight, so pruning moves them toward training’s preferred values.

r003.rationale: It describes the mask as encoding signal gathered from a full training run and calls producing it an optimization step, implying that finding tickets at initialization without that training signal is harder than it might seem.

astra-6.text:
The key idea is that the mask isn’t independent of the data. In the usual lottery ticket procedure, you train a network, identify which weights to keep, and then reset those weights to their initial values. So the weights are back at initialization, but the choice of which weights survive was made using information from training.

That means resetting the weights doesn’t reset everything you’ve learned. Some of that information is encoded in the mask. You can think of the mask as a set of binary parameters: instead of changing a weight’s value, you decide whether it’s on or off. Choosing those parameters based on the task is itself a form of training.

So the distinction is between weights that haven’t been trained and a subnetwork that hasn’t been selected using training. Those aren’t the same thing.

r001.rationale: It describes selecting and resetting retained weights, but does not state that the resulting subnetwork achieves above-chance accuracy before further training.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret zeroing small-magnitude weights as moving them toward values training would have produced.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that finding lottery tickets at initialization without prior dense-model training may be harder than expected.

sol-6.1.text:
What I mean is that choosing which weights to keep is itself a way of learning. We tend to think of training as changing the values of the weights, and pruning as just removing some of them. But if you use information from the task to decide which connections survive, then the resulting mask encodes information about that task.

So even if the surviving weights are reset to their initial values, you haven’t necessarily returned to an untrained system. The weights might be at initialization, but the connectivity has been selected through a learning process. You’ve effectively optimized a set of binary parameters: whether each connection is on or off.

That doesn’t mean the lottery ticket result isn’t interesting. It means we should distinguish between learning the weight values and learning which weights to use. A network can benefit from training through either of those channels.

r001.rationale: The response says task-selected connectivity can encode learning even after weights are reset, but does not state that a magnitude-pruned, rewound subnetwork achieves above-chance accuracy before further training.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret zeroing small-magnitude weights as moving them toward values training would have produced.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the difficulty of identifying lottery tickets at initialization without prior dense-model training.
